questions.sub_skill: Implement conditional access for Microsoft Entra Agent ID
questions.prompt: Your tenant requires MFA for All users. You deploy your first autonomous agent and it fails to acquire a token. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The agent's blueprint lacks a client secret; issue one
Agents cannot satisfy interactive controls such as MFA — exclude agent identities from the broad policy and write dedicated agent policies using identity filters, risk and named locations
Conditional Access does not apply to agents at all; the failure is unrelated
The agent needs a Global Secure Access licence before it can acquire tokens
questions.explanation: There is no human to complete an MFA challenge. Microsoft's guidance is to audit broad policies for agent impact, exclude agents, and build dedicated policies from controls agents can actually satisfy. Conditional Access does apply to agent identities requesting tokens for a resource.
why_not: A client secret does not help. The failure is the MFA requirement, which no credential lets an agent satisfy.
Conditional Access does apply to agent identities requesting tokens for a resource - that is exactly why the broad MFA policy caught the agent.
No licence lets an agent complete an MFA challenge. There is no human to complete it.

questions.sub_skill: Analyze blast radius for security risks related to Entra Agent ID by using Defender XDR
questions.prompt: Two agents have identical tools and grounding sources. One runs on-behalf-of a signed-in user; the other is autonomous. How do their blast radii compare?
options: Identical, because the tools are identical
The autonomous agent's is larger in every case
The on-behalf-of agent's varies with whoever is talking to it, because it acts with that user's permissions; the autonomous agent's is fixed at whatever its own identity holds
Neither has a blast radius until a credential is compromised
questions.explanation: An on-behalf-of agent acts with the signed-in user's identity and permissions, so its reach changes per user. An autonomous agent has no user context, so its own assignments are the whole of its reach. Blast radius here is about subversion of instructions, not credential theft.
why_not: Identical tools do not mean identical reach. The on-behalf-of agent acts with each user's permissions, so its reach changes per user.
Not in every case. An on-behalf-of agent serving a highly privileged user can reach more than an autonomous agent with narrow assignments.
Blast radius here is about subverting the agent's instructions, not stealing a credential. It exists as soon as the agent can act.

questions.sub_skill: Enable and configure real-time protection for Microsoft Copilot Studio agents
questions.prompt: You enable advanced real-time protection in the Microsoft Defender portal. Agents remain unprotected. What is missing, and what would have told you?
options: A Copilot Studio licence; the agent would show as Unlicensed
The corresponding Power Platform administrator step; a protected agent shows as Connected in the Security for AI settings
An Entra Agent ID blueprint; the agent would not appear in the inventory
A Defender for Cloud Apps connector; the agent would show as Discovered
questions.explanation: Advanced real-time protection is a two-sided configuration. The Defender portal step and the Power Platform step are both required, and the indicator that protection is live is the agent showing as Connected in the Security for AI settings.
why_not: Licensing is not the missing piece. Advanced real-time protection needs both the Defender portal step and the Power Platform step.
An agent's identity blueprint is not what enables runtime protection. The missing half is the Power Platform administrator step.
A Defender for Cloud Apps connector is not what is missing. The configuration needs the Power Platform step, and the agent showing as Connected in the Security for AI settings confirms it.

questions.prompt: An agent created eight months ago by a departed employee still runs nightly with nobody accountable. Which mechanisms should have prevented this?
options: A Conditional Access policy blocking high-risk agent identities
An entitlement management access package with an expiry, plus a sponsorship lifecycle workflow that transfers sponsorship when a sponsor leaves
Advanced real-time protection on the agent's runtime
Assigning the agent to a dedicated Security Copilot workspace
questions.explanation: Access packages make an agent's access expire unless someone re-confirms it, and lifecycle workflow templates for sponsorship transfer exist specifically to prevent orphaned agents. Conditional Access governs how an agent gets tokens, not who is accountable for it.
why_not: Conditional Access governs how an agent gets tokens, not who is accountable for it.
Runtime protection inspects what an agent does while it runs. It does not expire access or transfer ownership.
A Security Copilot workspace has nothing to do with an agent's ownership or access expiry.

questions.sub_skill: Manage agents in Microsoft 365 admin center
questions.prompt: Any licensed user in your tenant can build a Copilot Studio agent. Where do you take a tenant-wide inventory and block ones you do not want?
options: Entra admin center, under Agent ID blueprints
Microsoft 365 admin center agent management
Defender portal, under Security for AI agents
Power Platform admin center environments only
questions.explanation: The Microsoft 365 admin center provides the tenant-wide agent inventory with ownership, risk indicators, and the ability to block or disable. Shadow agents are the governance problem here, and you cannot govern an inventory you have not taken.
why_not: Agent ID blueprints are identity constructs in Entra. The tenant-wide agent inventory with block and disable is in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
The Defender portal is where runtime protection is configured, not where the tenant-wide inventory with block and disable lives.
Power Platform environments are only part of the picture. The tenant-wide inventory is in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
